solution:
(a) (i) The electric force between an electron and a proton at a distance \(r\) apart is:
\(F_e = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}\)
where the negative sign indicates that the force is attractive. The corresponding gravitational force (always attractive) is:
\(F_G = -G\frac{m_p m_e}{r^{2}}\)
where \(m_p\) and \(m_e\) are the masses of a proton and an electron respectively.
\(\left|\frac{F_e}{F_G}\right| = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 G m_p m_e} = 2.3 \times 10^{39}\) [NCERT prints \(2.4 \times 10^{39}\); with \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) the value is \(2.27 \times 10^{39}\).]
(ii) On similar lines, the ratio of the magnitudes of electric force to the gravitational force between two protons at a distance \(r\) apart is:
\(\left|\frac{F_e}{F_G}\right| = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 G m_p m_p} = 1.2 \times 10^{36}\) [NCERT prints \(1.3 \times 10^{36}\); the value is \(1.24 \times 10^{36}\).]
However, it may be mentioned here that the signs of the two forces are different. For two protons, the gravitational force is attractive in nature and the Coulomb force is repulsive. The actual values of these forces between two protons inside a nucleus (distance between two protons is \(\sim 10^{-15}\,\text{m}\) inside a nucleus) are \(F_e \sim 230\,\text{N}\), whereas, \(F_G \sim 1.9 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{N}\).
The (dimensionless) ratio of the two forces shows that electrical forces are enormously stronger than the gravitational forces.
(b) The electric force \(\mathbf{F}\) exerted by a proton on an electron is same in magnitude to the force exerted by an electron on a proton; however, the masses of an electron and a proton are different. Thus, the magnitude of force is
\(|\mathbf{F}| = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}} = 8.987 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C})^{2} / (10^{-10}\,\text{m})^{2} = 2.3 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{N}\)
Using Newton's second law of motion, \(F = ma\), the acceleration that an electron will undergo is
\(a = 2.3 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{N} / 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg} = 2.5 \times 10^{22}\,\text{m/s}^{2}\)
Comparing this with the value of acceleration due to gravity, we can conclude that the effect of gravitational field is negligible on the motion of electron and it undergoes very large accelerations under the action of Coulomb force due to a proton.
The value for acceleration of the proton is
\(2.3 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{N} / 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg} = 1.4 \times 10^{19}\,\text{m/s}^{2}\)
note: ke^2/(G mp me) = 2.27e39, printed 2.4e39. ke^2/(G mp^2) = 1.24e36, printed 1.3e36.

solution:
(a) Field at P due to charge \(+10\,\mu\text{C}\)
\(= \frac{10^{-5}\,\text{C}}{4\pi(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2})} \times \frac{1}{(15-0.25)^{2} \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}}\)
\(= 4.13 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along BP
Field at P due to charge \(-10\,\mu\text{C}\)
\(= \frac{10^{-5}\,\text{C}}{4\pi(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2})} \times \frac{1}{(15+0.25)^{2} \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}}\)
\(= 3.86 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along PA
The resultant electric field at P due to the two charges at A and B is \(= 2.7 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along BP.
In this example, the ratio OP/OB is quite large \((= 60)\). Thus, we can expect to get approximately the same result as above by directly using the formula for electric field at a far-away point on the axis of a dipole. For a dipole consisting of charges \(\pm q\), \(2a\) distance apart, the electric field at a distance \(r\) from the centre on the axis of the dipole has a magnitude
\(E = \frac{2p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{3}}\)   \((r/a \gg 1)\)
where \(p = 2a\,q\) is the magnitude of the dipole moment.
The direction of electric field on the dipole axis is always along the direction of the dipole moment vector (i.e., from \(-q\) to \(q\)). Here, \(p = 10^{-5}\,\text{C} \times 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m} = 5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C m}\)
Therefore,
\(E = \frac{2 \times 5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C m}}{4\pi(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2})} \times \frac{1}{(15)^{3} \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}} = 2.7 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\)
along the dipole moment direction AB, which is close to the result obtained earlier.
(b) Field at Q due to charge \(+10\,\mu\text{C}\) at B
\(= \frac{10^{-5}\,\text{C}}{4\pi(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2})} \times \frac{1}{[15^{2} + (0.25)^{2}] \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}}\)
\(= 3.99 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along BQ
Field at Q due to charge \(-10\,\mu\text{C}\) at A
\(= \frac{10^{-5}\,\text{C}}{4\pi(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2})} \times \frac{1}{[15^{2} + (0.25)^{2}] \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}}\)
\(= 3.99 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along QA.
Clearly, the components of these two forces with equal magnitudes cancel along the direction OQ but add up along the direction parallel to BA. Therefore, the resultant electric field at Q due to the two charges at A and B is
\(= 2 \times \frac{0.25}{\sqrt{15^{2} + (0.25)^{2}}} \times 3.99 \times 10^{6}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along BA
\(= 1.33 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\) along BA.
As in (a), we can expect to get approximately the same result by directly using the formula for dipole field at a point on the normal to the axis of the dipole:
\(E = \frac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{3}}\)   \((r/a \gg 1)\)
\(= \frac{5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C m}}{4\pi(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2})} \times \frac{1}{(15)^{3} \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}}\)
\(= 1.33 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\).
The direction of electric field in this case is opposite to the direction of the dipole moment vector. Again, the result agrees with that obtained before.

(a) Since the electric field has only an \(x\) component, for faces perpendicular to \(x\) direction, the angle between \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\Delta\mathbf{S}\) is \(\pm \pi/2\). Therefore, the flux \(\phi = \mathbf{E}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{S}\) is separately zero for each face of the cube except the two shaded ones. Now the magnitude of the electric field at the left face is
\(E_L = \alpha x^{1/2} = \alpha a^{1/2}\)
\((x = a\) at the left face).
The magnitude of electric field at the right face is
\(E_R = \alpha x^{1/2} = \alpha (2a)^{1/2}\)
\((x = 2a\) at the right face).
The corresponding fluxes are
\(\phi_L = \mathbf{E}_L\cdot\Delta\mathbf{S} = \Delta S\,\mathbf{E}_L\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_L = E_L\,\Delta S\cos\theta = -E_L\,\Delta S\), since \(\theta = 180^\circ\)
\(= -E_L\,a^{2}\)
\(\phi_R = \mathbf{E}_R\cdot\Delta\mathbf{S} = E_R\,\Delta S\cos\theta = E_R\,\Delta S\), since \(\theta = 0^\circ\)
\(= E_R\,a^{2}\)
Net flux through the cube
\(= \phi_R + \phi_L = E_R\,a^{2} - E_L\,a^{2} = a^{2}(E_R - E_L) = \alpha a^{2}\left[(2a)^{1/2} - a^{1/2}\right]\)
\(= \alpha a^{5/2}\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)\)
\(= 800\,(0.1)^{5/2}\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)\)
\(= 1.05\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)
(b) We can use Gauss's law to find the total charge \(q\) inside the cube. We have \(\phi = q/\varepsilon_0\) or \(q = \phi\varepsilon_0\). Therefore,
\(q = 1.05 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C} = 9.30 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}\).

In the STEADY STATE no current flows through the capacitor branch, because a fully charged capacitor passes nothing. So the current circulates only in the loop containing the cells and the two resistors, and the capacitor branch is a dead end whose voltage we read off at the end.
THE CURRENT. Going round the conducting loop, the 2V cell drives against the V cell, and the two resistors R and 2R are in series:
\(2V - V = i(2R + R)\)
\(V = 3iR \quad\Longrightarrow\quad i = \dfrac{V}{3R}\)
(i) POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN P AND Q. Travelling from P to Q along the branch containing the cell V and the resistor R, and adding up the changes:
\(V_{P} - V_{Q} = -V - iR = -V - \left(\dfrac{V}{3R}\right)R = -V - \dfrac{V}{3}\)
\(V_{P} - V_{Q} = -\dfrac{4V}{3}\)
(ii) POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE ACROSS THE CAPACITOR. Now travel from P to Q along the OTHER branch, the one containing the cell V and the capacitor C. Since P and Q are the same two points, the total must agree with what we just found:
\(V_{P} - V_{Q} = -V + V_{C}\)
\(-\dfrac{4V}{3} = -V + V_{C}\)
\(V_{C} = -\dfrac{4V}{3} + V\)
\(V_{C} = -\dfrac{V}{3}\)
The potential difference across the capacitor is \(\dfrac{V}{3}\) in magnitude, the sign showing which plate is at the higher potential.
The method is the one to remember for any steady-state RC network: find the current in the purely conducting loop first, ignoring the capacitor entirely, then get the capacitor's voltage by equating two routes between the SAME pair of nodes. No current flows through C, so no IR drop occurs in its branch and the whole of the branch's voltage sits across the capacitor.
note: The line read -V + V/3 (= -2V/3) before the correct -4V/3 + V.

solution:
There is NO external resistor here: the three cells are simply joined in parallel to one another, so any current that leaves one cell must enter the others. Since the net current drawn from the combination is zero, the common terminal voltage V is just the equivalent emf of the parallel combination:
\(V = \dfrac{\dfrac{\varepsilon_{A}}{r_{A}} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_{B}}{r_{B}} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_{C}}{r_{C}}}{\dfrac{1}{r_{A}} + \dfrac{1}{r_{B}} + \dfrac{1}{r_{C}}}\)
As the question labels them, A is the 2 V cell with \(r = 5\ \Omega\), B the 3 V cell with \(r = 5\ \Omega\) and C the 5 V cell with \(r = 1\ \Omega\):
\(V = \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{1} + \dfrac{3}{5} + \dfrac{2}{5}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5}} = \dfrac{6}{1{\cdot}4} = \dfrac{30}{7}\ \mathrm{V}\)
Now each cell's current follows from \(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon - V}{r}\), and its SIGN says whether the cell is being discharged or charged.
CELL C (5 V):
\(I_{C} = \dfrac{5 - \dfrac{30}{7}}{1} = \dfrac{5}{7}\ \mathrm{A}\) approximately \(0{\cdot}71\) A
CELL B (3 V):
\(I_{B} = \dfrac{3 - \dfrac{30}{7}}{5} = -\dfrac{9}{35}\ \mathrm{A}\) approximately \(0{\cdot}26\) A
CELL A (2 V):
\(I_{A} = \dfrac{2 - \dfrac{30}{7}}{5} = -\dfrac{16}{35}\ \mathrm{A}\) approximately \(0{\cdot}46\) A
So the 5 V cell DISCHARGES at \(\dfrac{5}{7}\) A while the 3 V and 2 V cells are being CHARGED, at \(\dfrac{9}{35}\) A and \(\dfrac{16}{35}\) A. The books balance exactly:
\(\dfrac{9}{35} + \dfrac{16}{35} = \dfrac{25}{35} = \dfrac{5}{7}\)
This is why cells of unequal emf should not be paralleled in practice: the strongest one drives current backwards through the others.
note: The working had relabelled A and C (A as the 5 V cell); the stem makes A the 2 V cell and C the 5 V cell.
